For the owner · Lady Birds Cafe · 120 W Center St, Sheridan

A website for Lady Birds,
already built.

Not a proposal, not a mock-up on a slide. The site is finished and working. This packet shows you what it looks like on every screen, what it does, how people will find it, how it works with your Facebook page, and where it could go from here. Nothing is owed and nothing is signed.

Built on spec Not published Yours to look at

First · Who did this, and why

We have been eating here for a year.

My family and I moved to Sheridan about a year ago. Lady Birds is one of the first places we found that we kept coming back to.

When you land somewhere new, you spend the first few months working out where to eat. You try everything on the square. Most places you go once. A handful you go back to, and after a while those become the places you take people when they visit — the ones you name when somebody asks. Lady Birds became one of ours pretty quickly.

Somewhere in that first year I went looking for your hours online, the way you do when you are already in the truck. What I found were listings on other people's websites, and a Facebook page doing a lot of work on its own. Nothing that belonged to you.

Websites are only half of what I do. The other half is the software underneath — the systems that take the orders, hold the schedule, count what is left in the walk-in, and add up the week. The part customers see and the part that does the work, built by the same pair of hands.

So I built this one on my own time, without being asked, because I wanted to see what this place would look like done properly. Everything in this packet already exists and works. If you like it, I would be glad to hand it over and look after it. If you do not, you have lost nothing and I got to spend a weekend on a project I enjoyed.

Either way, thank you for the chicken fried steak.

01 · The front page

Your building, your logo, your street.

The first thing a visitor sees is your storefront on Center Street with your own logo over it — and right beside it, the three things they came for: whether you are open right now, where you are, and the phone number. No menu to dig through, no scrolling required.

02 · Every screen

Computer, tablet, phone.

The same site rearranges itself for whatever it is opened on. Nothing is cut and nothing is buried behind a menu button — on all three, the hours, the address and the call button sit on the first screen before anyone scrolls.

On a phone there is one extra touch: a bar pinned to the bottom of the screen with Call, Hours and Directions. It stays put the whole time someone is reading, so your phone number is never more than one thumb-reach away.

03 · What it does

The working parts.

Calling

One tap dials you

Every Call button opens the phone dialer with your number already in it. No copying, no typing.

Directions

Straight into their maps

Directions hands off to Google Maps or Apple Maps with the route already set from wherever they are standing.

Hours

It knows what day it is

The site reads the visitor's own clock and shows today's hours, with the current day marked on the week's board. Nobody has to work out whether Tuesday is the closed one.

Food

The plates, photographed

Chicken fried steak, the catfish tray, firecracker tacos and the Caribbean salmon — real photographs of real plates, not stock pictures of somebody else's food.

Map

Across from the courthouse

A live map on the Visit page, plus the parking note, for anyone who has never been to the square.

Speed

Loads before they give up

Photographs are delivered in modern formats and sized to the screen asking for them — a phone on a country signal never downloads the desktop-sized picture.

Everyone

Readable by anyone

It works with screen readers, every photograph is described, the text passes contrast standards, and the whole site can be operated from a keyboard.

Home screen

Save it like an app

A regular can add it to their phone's home screen and it sits there with your logo as the icon — the convenience of an app, with nothing to download.

Upkeep

Nothing to maintain

No plugins to update, no software that expires, no login to forget. It sits there and works.

04 · Being found

What search engines see.

A website is not only a page for people — it is also what Google reads when somebody in Grant County types catfish near me. This one was built to be read properly.

1

Machine-readable business facts

Your name, street address, phone number, opening hours and the fact that this is a restaurant are written into the page in the exact format Google publishes for it. That is what lets a search result show your hours right there in the listing.

2

Every page titled and described

Home, Menu and Visit each carry their own title and summary, so a search result reads like an invitation instead of a web address.

3

Shares that look like something

Pasted into Facebook or a text message, the link opens out with a photograph and a proper description instead of a bare blue line.

4

Written in plain structure

Real headings in a sensible order, and a written description on every photograph. Good for search engines for the same reason it is good for a blind customer.

5

Fast, and built for phones first

Google measures both and counts them. This is a light site built for a phone from the ground up, not a desktop page squeezed down.

An honest word about search. None of this is a magic switch. Results build over weeks, and for a local restaurant the single biggest factor is a claimed, filled-in Google Business Profile. The site makes that profile stronger and gives it somewhere to point — the two work together. Anyone who promises you the top spot is selling something.

05 · Site and social together

Facebook is the conversation. The site is the address.

You rent your Facebook page. You would own your website. They do different jobs, and they are stronger pointed at each other.

Your Facebook page is already doing real work — specials, the days you close early, photographs customers leave. That is the living part, and the site does not try to replace it. It links straight to it and says plainly that specials go up there first.

What Facebook cannot do is be found by someone who has never heard of you. Somebody driving through Grant County looking for lunch does not search Facebook — they search Google, or they ask their phone out loud. A page inside a social network is largely invisible to that search. A website is exactly what it is looking for.

Facebook does

Today

Specials, closures, a new plate, the crowd on a Friday. Things that change and want a comment section.

The site does

Always

Hours, address, phone, what you serve. The facts somebody needs at 11 am with one hand on the wheel.

Together

A loop

Search finds the site, the site sends them to Facebook and they follow you; your posts link back to the site, which lifts it in search. Each one feeds the other.

There is a practical safety net in it too. Pages get locked out, hacked, or caught by a rule change, and there is no phone number to call when it happens. If that ever happened to yours, everything a customer actually needs would still be sitting at your own address, untouched.

07 · What it opens up

The door this puts in the wall.

None of the following is built, and none of it is needed for the site to do its job. But once a restaurant has its own place on the internet, each of these stops being a big project and becomes a small addition. Every one of them is something I build and look after myself — the website and the software under it come from the same bench, so there is never a second company to chase. This is the part worth thinking about slowly.

First

Knowing what happens

How many people looked, what they tapped, what day and hour, whether they were in Sheridan or two towns over. Real numbers instead of a guess.

First

The menu you update yourself

Change a price or add a special from your phone and the site updates. No calling anybody.

First

A table QR code

The same menu on the table, always current, never reprinted.

Next

Rewards that remember

A punch card that lives on a phone instead of a wallet, and tells you who your regulars actually are.

Next

Scheduling

The week's roster posted once and visible to everybody, with no group text and nobody claiming they never saw it.

Next

Shift swaps

A server puts a shift up, someone takes it, you approve it — on your phone, with a record of who agreed to what.

Next

Inventory that counts down

What is on hand, what is running out, what you ordered last month and what it cost. The end of the walk-in clipboard.

Later

Call-ahead and waitlist

Orders taken before they arrive; a Friday queue that texts people when the table is ready instead of holding them in the doorway.

Later

Catering and big tables

A form for the church lunch or the ball team, arriving as one clear message instead of a half-heard phone call.

Later

Gift cards

Sold from the site, redeemed at the counter. Christmas mostly runs itself.

Later

A list you own

Customers who ask to hear from you, reachable by text or email without paying to reach your own followers.

Later

Reviews, gathered

A gentle nudge to happy customers at the right moment, pointed where it counts for search.

The order matters more than the list. Analytics first, because it tells you which of the others is worth doing. Everything after that becomes a decision made with evidence instead of a hunch.

08 · What is still needed

Three short conversations.

1

Your hours, from you

What is on the site came from public listings, and one of them disagrees about Sunday. Five minutes with you settles it for good.

2

A menu

A photograph of the printed menu is enough. Right now the site shows only dishes there are real photographs of, and carries no prices anywhere.

3

The photographs

The food and dining room pictures are from the Arkansas Living article, taken by Rob Roedel. They are fine for showing you an idea. Before the site goes public they need his permission or replacing — and honestly, phone photographs taken on your own tables in good light would do the job well.

A note to finish

Before this I spent twenty-five years as a senior director and a senior business analyst, and now I run a small business myself. Those years taught me how a place actually makes and loses money. This last stretch has taught me what it feels like when the bills land on your own desk instead of somebody else's.

So here is the one thing I hold to. My price will always be fair and manageable for a business this size, and you will hear the number before any work starts. Costs are real. Taxes are real. And in the small-business world there is hardly ever anybody actually trying to help — mostly there is somebody trying to sell you a subscription.

I would like to work with you at a discounted rate. Not as a favor and not as a trial — I would rather have a neighbor I keep doing good work for than a one-time invoice. Put your name in front of the people already searching for lunch and bring more of them through the door. Then keep going: tighten the cost of goods line, and take some of the week's busywork off your hands.

There is no obligation attached to any of this, and no invoice behind it. I made it because I live here now and I would rather the places I like do well. If you want it, it is yours to talk about. If you want to think about it for a month, that is fine too — it is not going anywhere.

And if you ever just want somebody to explain what any of this actually means, in plain words, with no sales pitch on the end, call me for that. I am five minutes away.
